worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=x\cdot \frac{1}{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\cdot \frac{1}{t})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & =\frac{1}{t}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{t})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & =\frac{1}{t}-\frac{x}{{t}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-\frac{1}{t} & =-\frac{x}{{t}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t} & =(\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{{t}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t({t}^{2}-1)}{{t}^{2}-x} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t({t}^{2}-1)}{{t}^{2}-x}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{t({t}^{2}-1)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} \\ t({t}^{2}-1)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & ={t}^{2}-x \\ t({t}^{2}-1)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x & ={t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t({t}^{2}-1)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} & =\frac{t}{{t}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{1}{t({t}^{2}-1)},\,Q(t)=\frac{t}{{t}^{2}-1}.
$$
html:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form y=xf(y′)+g(y′), where f and g are differentiable functions of y′.

In our case, we wish to transform the equation y=x⋅1(dydx)+dydx into a first-order linear equation for x=x(t). We proceed in three steps:

Step 1: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to x.

We have the substitution t=dydx.

Substituting this into the equation gives y=x⋅1t+t.

Differentiating both sides with respect to x, we have ddx(y)=ddx(x⋅1t+t).

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get dydx=ddx(x⋅1t)+ddx(t)t=1tddx(x)+xddx(1t)+ddx(t)t=1t−xt2dtdx+dtdx.

Step 2: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate dtdx as follows:

t−1t=−xt2dtdx+dtdxt2−1t=(t2−xt2)dtdxt(t2−1)t2−x=dtdx which gives dtdx=t(t2−1)t2−x.

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have dxdt=t2−xt(t2−1).

Step 3: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form dxdt+P(t)x=Q(t) as follows: dxdt=t2−xt(t2−1)t(t2−1)dxdt=t2−xt(t2−1)dxdt+x=t2dxdt+xt(t2−1)=t2t(t2−1)dxdt+xt(t2−1)=tt2−1

Therefore, we conclude that P(t)=1t(t2−1),Q(t)=tt2−1.
